questions.question: Using the described monopolist's graph — equilibrium at 80 units where marginal cost crosses marginal revenue, price R200 on the demand curve, average cost R160 — explain why the equilibrium sits where it does, calculate the total economic profit in full marking style, and explain what the identical method would show if the cost and price positions were reversed.
questions.expected_answer: Equilibrium sits where marginal cost equals marginal revenue because up to that output each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, and beyond it each extra unit costs more than it earns — so 80 units maximises profit. The price is then read UP from that quantity to the demand curve, giving R200, which exceeds marginal revenue because selling an extra unit forces the price down on all units. Calculation in full marking style: profit per unit = price − average cost = R200 − R160 = R40; total economic profit = R40 × 80 units = R3 200, labelled as economic profit in rands. The setup line, the subtraction, the multiplication and the labelled answer each carry marks — a naked number forfeits the method marks. If the positions were reversed, with average cost at R200 and price at R160, the identical chain would give R160 − R200 = −R40 per unit and −R40 × 80 = an economic loss of R3 200. The procedure never changes; only the direction of the gap between price and average cost does.

questions.question: Using the practice table — the consumer price index at 130,0 last year and 139,1 this year, with a mini-basket of food weighted 50 percent up 8 percent, transport weighted 30 percent up 5 percent, and education weighted 20 percent up 3 percent — calculate the inflation rate and the weighted average increase in full marking style, and explain what the weighting reveals about how different households experience inflation.
questions.expected_answer: Inflation rate = (new index − old index) ÷ old index × 100 = (139,1 − 130,0) ÷ 130,0 × 100 = 9,1 ÷ 130,0 × 100 = 7,0 percent. The classic trap is dividing by the new index; the divisor is always the OLD index because a rate measures growth from where prices started. Weighted average increase = (0,5 × 8) + (0,3 × 5) + (0,2 × 3) = 4,0 + 1,5 + 0,6 = 6,1 percent. Full marks in both require the formula line, the substitution, and the final answer labelled as a percentage. The weighting reveals that the headline number is an average built on a particular basket: food's heavy weight drags the outcome toward food's price experience, so a household whose real basket is even more food-heavy — typically a low-income household — lives an inflation harsher than the published rate, while a household spending proportionally more on lightly weighted, slowly rising categories experiences less. Inflation is one number in print but many numbers in life, which is why distributional effects belong in any evaluation of it.

questions.question: Plan this session's thirty-mark practice essay 'Compare and contrast perfect competition and monopoly, and use a described graph to explain the monopoly's long-run equilibrium position', naming what earns the marks in each structural part.
questions.expected_answer: Definition opening (2): a market structure describes how a market is organised — the number of sellers, the nature of the product and the ease of entry; no borrowed question wording. Main body (20): paired contrasts at two marks per developed pair — very many firms against one; identical products against a unique product without close substitutes; free entry against barriers of scale, licences and patents; price takers against a price maker still bound by demand; a horizontal individual demand curve against a downward-sloping one with marginal revenue below it; long-run normal profit as entry competes gains away against persistent economic profit behind barriers; efficiency pressure against restricted output at a higher price; fresh produce markets against the electricity grid as examples. The graph paragraph in words: long-run monopoly equilibrium sits where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, price stands above on the demand curve, and because barriers hold, price can remain above average cost, leaving the rectangle of economic profit. Evaluation (6): scale economies can justify regulated natural monopolies, but unregulated monopoly transfers welfare from consumers and dulls innovation, which is why competition authorities police dominance and collusion — a balanced verdict with South African anchors. Closing judgement (2): one fresh line, such as that structure shapes conduct, so policy watches structure.
